title: Subuddhi Raya
html:
A Former Governor of Gauda

Among those whom Sri Chaitanya favoured with special mercy is a man who met Him only once: Subuddhi Raya. The “Charitamrita” calls him Subuddhi Raya, and more often simply Raya; the biographies likewise call him Sri Subuddhi Raya.1 His life is remembered not for the worldly position he once held, but because Mahaprabhu received him, heard him out and gave him what no rules could give — and for the way he then served the Gosvamis and the Vaishnavas of Vraja.

By birth he was a brahmana, known for his learning in the scriptures. The “Charitamrita” does not name his varna outright; the story shows only that he was a Hindu of high caste, since the Shah's wife demands that he be deprived of his Hindu caste. The sources name neither his parents nor his birthplace; the year and day of his appearance and of his departure are unknown, and his days are not in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

In earlier days Subuddhi Raya was a governor — an adhikari, an official holding authority — in Gauda.2 Gauda was what the old capital of Bengal was called, and from it the whole region took its name.3 In his service at that time was one Hussain — Saiyad Hussain Khan, who was destined to become the Badshah of Gauda, Hussain Shah:

“Formerly, when Subuddhi Raya was a governor (adhikari) in Gauda, Saiyad Husain Khan was in his service.” (CC, Madhya 25.180)

One of the biographies calls Hussain his protégé; another in one place says the opposite — that Subuddhi served under Hussain — but this contradicts both the “Charitamrita” and that biography's own account.4

The Whip and the Water Pot

Krishnadasa Kaviraja tells the story that brought Subuddhi to Mahaprabhu as follows:

“Raya put him in charge (munsiph) of digging a large pond; finding a fault in his work, Raya struck him with a whip. Later, when Husain Khan became king of Gauda, he greatly advanced Subuddhi Raya. His wife saw the marks of the whipping on his body and urged the king to have Subuddhi Raya killed. The king said, ‘Raya has been my patron; he is a father to me. That I should kill him — such talk is not right.’ His wife said, ‘If you will not take his life, then take his caste.’ The king said, ‘If his caste is taken, he will not survive.’ His wife threatened to die, and the king was caught in a dilemma. At last he had water from a Muslim's water pot (karoya) put into Subuddhi Raya's mouth.” (CC, Madhya 25.181–186)

The pond was a large one (dighi); it was Subuddhi himself who undertook to have it dug, setting Hussain to supervise the work (munsiph), and the fault for which Hussain felt the whip across his back was no small one. In time Hussain became Badshah of Gauda,5 but he did not forget his former benefactor: out of gratitude he honoured Subuddhi highly and, as one of the biographies remarks, bore him no grudge for the whipping. The scars, however, remained on the Shah's back. Seeing them, the Begum questioned her husband and learned that it was Subuddhi who had beaten him in the days when he was governor. The Shah refused to execute his benefactor; he refused, too, to strip him of his caste, knowing that for Subuddhi this would be as good as death.6 Only when his wife threatened to kill herself did the Shah, seeing no way out, have water from a karoya — a pot that Muslims use for their water — poured into his mouth: water that Muslims had touched. By the smarta custom of the time this alone was enough for a Hindu to lose his caste. For a Vaishnava, however, such a loss is nothing before the holy name, and, as we shall see, the Lord Himself would prescribe for Subuddhi nothing but the Name.

In Varanasi: the Name Instead of Atonement

Subuddhi had long wished to give up worldly affairs. He took the loss of caste as a pretext (chadma): leaving behind his family and all worldly concerns, he went to Varanasi. It was not resentment or humiliation that made him renounced — he merely used the loss of caste as an occasion to leave a world to which his heart had long grown cold.

In Varanasi he asked the smarta panditas what atonement (prayashchitta) he should perform. They told him to drink boiling ghee and so give up his life.7 Other brahmanas objected that the fault was not so grave as to be paid for with his life. The disagreement of the learned left Subuddhi confused, and he hesitated:

“He asked the panditas what atonement he should perform. They said, ‘Drink boiling ghee and give up your life.’ Another said, ‘Not so: the fault is slight.’ Hearing this, Raya was left in doubt.” (CC, Madhya 25.188–189)

This very disagreement shows the futility of the smartas' prayashchittas: some of the learned demand death, others reject it, and neither can give the soul peace.

Then Mahaprabhu came to Kashi. Subuddhi came to Him and told Him everything in order. The Lord did not choose between the panditas' opinions, nor did He give him another, milder prayashchitta — He gave him the Name:

“Then, when Mahaprabhu came to Varanasi, Raya met Him and told Him his story. The Lord said, ‘Go from here to Vrindavana and always chant the name of Krishna in sankirtana. By the mere semblance of the holy name (namabhasa) your sin and its taint will go; and by chanting the Name itself you will attain Krishna's feet. Chanting Krishna's name further, you will dwell in Krishna's abode. This is the atonement even for the greatest sins.’” (CC, Madhya 25.190–193)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Anubhashya” heads these verses thus: the Lord gives an injunction better than all others; the fruits of namabhasa and of the pure Name are different. Sin departs at the mere semblance of the Name, its passing shadow; the Name itself leads further, to Krishna's feet and a place in His abode. The Lord speaks the word “atonement” to a man who had come to Him seeking atonement, but for Him the Name is not a rite for cancelling sins, nor a means, but the goal itself: where the Name is chanted, the question of atonement simply falls away. Thus Mahaprabhu freed Subuddhi from the search for a prayashchitta, and rejected the counsel of suicide — just as later He would hold Sanatana Gosvami back from it (CC, Antya 4).

The Woodcutter of Mathura

Having received the order, Subuddhi set out for Vrindavana by way of Prayaga and Ayodhya and stayed some days in Naimisharanya. Meanwhile the Lord, having visited Vrindavana, had left it for Prayaga. Coming to Mathura, Subuddhi found the Lord already gone, and was deeply grieved (CC, Madhya 25.194–196). In this separation true renunciation (vairagya) and indifference to everything worldly awoke in him; one of the biographies writes that in the grief of deep separation he took up severe renunciation.

This is how he lived:

“Raya would gather dry wood and sell it in Mathura, earning five or six paisa a bundle. He himself lived on one paisa's worth of chickpeas and kept the rest of his money with a merchant. Whenever he saw a poor Vaishnava, he fed him; and when Gaudiyas came, he gave them yogurt and rice and had them massaged with oil.” (CC, Madhya 25.197–199)

The dry wood he gathered in the forest himself, with great labour. What he earned he did not spend on himself alone: with these few coins he fed other Vaishnavas too, and to the Gaudiyas who came to Vraja he gave yogurt with rice and oil to anoint their bodies.8 His life shows that it is not only the rich who can render service to Vishnu and the Vaishnavas: where there is a sincere wish to serve, then even in poverty, as the Lord wills, nothing that service requires is lacking.

Rupa Gosvami's Companion

Meanwhile Rupa Gosvami, who had received the Lord's teachings at Prayaga, came to Mathura:

“Meanwhile, when Rupa Gosani came to Mathura, Subuddhi Raya met him at Dhruva-ghata.” (CC, Madhya 25.179)

They had known each other since Gauda. Rupa rejoiced to see the renunciation of his old acquaintance and his eagerness to serve the Vaishnavas, and Subuddhi received him lovingly and became his guide:

“When Rupa Gosani came, Raya welcomed him with great affection, took him along and showed him the twelve forests.” (CC, Madhya 25.200)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta heads this verse the same way: Subuddhi shows Sri Rupa the twelve forests. Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” writes that Rupa with his brother Anupama, “taking the steadfast Subuddhi Raya as companion,” entered Vraja (15.28); and one of the biographies says that he guided both brothers through the forests of Vraja.9 Rupa stayed in Vrindavana only a month and then went in search of Sanatana: hearing that Mahaprabhu had come to Prayaga by the road along the Ganga, he and Anupama took the same way (CC, Madhya 25.201–202).

Meeting Sanatana Gosvami

Sanatana Gosvami, having received the Lord's teachings in Kashi, came to Prayaga and from there went on to Mathura by the main, royal road.10 There, in Mathura, Subuddhi Raya met him:

“In Mathura Subuddhi Raya met him and told him all the news of Rupa and Anupama. The two brothers went by the Ganga path and Sanatana by the royal road; that is why he did not meet them.” (CC, Madhya 25.204–205)11

Subuddhi, like Sanatana, had come to Vrindavana at Mahaprabhu's bidding.12 He had known Sanatana as a minister at the court of Gauda, loved him dearly and wished to serve him. He showed Sanatana great affection, as their former relations called for, but Sanatana would not accept an affection grown out of worldly ties (vyavahara-sneha, CC, Madhya 25.206): the great renunciant remained unmoved by it; one of the biographies explains this by Sanatana's humility — he did not wish to accept service from Subuddhi.13 Govinda-deva relates that on coming to Mathura Sanatana first of all met the people of Mathura and Subuddhi Raya and, hearing that his brothers had gone by the road to Prayaga, stayed there, content in their company (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 16.41).

In Vraja to the End

Subuddhi Raya passed the remainder of his days in Vraja. He lived in great humility together with the Gosvamis and, with renunciation and steadfastness, sang the name of Hari — thus fulfilling the order Mahaprabhu had given him in Kashi. When and where he left this world is not known.

It seems that the books of the next generation remember him too, under the name Subuddhi Mishra.14 The “Narottama-vilasa” tells of Lokanatha Gosvami wandering through Vrindavana: “Suddenly he heard from someone that Sri Subuddhi Mishra had come to Vrindavana,” and then Sri Rupa Gosvami came (1.87–88); there too Subuddhi Mishra is named among the Lord's companions of whom a brahmana told Narottama (2.60–67). The “Bhakti-ratnakara” twice glorifies him in its lists of blessing: “Glory to Sri Subuddhi Mishra and Sri Jiva Gosani!” (1.33) and “Glory to Sri Bhugarbha, Lokanatha and Shashthidhara! Glory to Sri Subuddhi Mishra and Sri Chandrashekhara!” (2.12). And Narahari, in a pada of prayer to Gaura's companions, sings:

“Subuddhi with Raghava, Bhugarbha, Sri Lokanatha, who wander in Vraja in the joy of prema — may I have attachment to these names, may the evil mind go far away, may a thrill pervade my whole body.” (pada of Narahari “Ei abhilasha mane…,” 18.9)

Significance

Subuddhi Raya saw Mahaprabhu only once, but that one meeting sufficed him for a lifetime. A worldly misfortune — the loss of caste, for which the experts in smriti could find no atonement but death — became a door for him: the Lord freed him from the search for a prayashchitta by giving him the name of Krishna, and separation from the Lord, whom he did not find in Mathura, made him truly renounced.

Yet his renunciation was not dry. The penniless woodcutter of Mathura fed poor Vaishnavas, gave hospitality to pilgrims from Gauda, lovingly served Rupa Gosvami by showing him the forests of Vraja, and met Sanatana with the same love; and he passed his remaining years beside the Gosvamis, in humility and in chanting the Name. So his life, made memorable only by Mahaprabhu's mercy, teaches that anyone with a sincere wish to serve can serve the Lord and His devotees: the rest the Lord Himself provides.

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Subuddhi Mishra of Amaipura, the father of Jayananda (the “Charitamrita” names a Subuddhi Mishra among the branches of the Lord's tree, Adi 10.111), and the Subuddhi Mishra whom the “Vaishnava-vandana” remembers among the devotees of Puri; a Subuddhi Mishra also appears in the list of companions in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (201) and in the genealogy of the “Prema-vilasa” (24.824), but who he is has not been established. In CC, Madhya 12.122 subuddhi is not a name but the word “intelligent” (said of the simple Bengali who washed the Lord's feet).
  2. The biographies call him the king (raja) of Gauda; according to one of them, he held this position for a short time when he was young. Another, in its chapter on Rupa, calls him, as the “Charitamrita” does, an adhikari. The verse CC, Madhya 25.180 reads gaude ‘adhikari’, “a governor (official) in Gauda”; it was Hussain who became king of Gauda (25.182: gaude ‘raja’ haila). We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  3. One of the biographies explains, citing the Bengali dictionary of Ashutosh Deb and Haridasa Dasa's “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana”: Gauda was the old capital of Bengal, in what is now Malda district. The “Skanda Purana” knows five Gaudas (pancha-gauda: Sarasvata, Kanyakubja, Utkala, Mithila and Bengal), but the name referred above all to the land between Vanga (Eastern Bengal) and Mithila. Vijaya Sena of Karnataka became king of Gauda (his descendants were called gaudeshvaras), and his son Ballala Sena founded Gauda as a city on the Ganga, whose course later shifted away. Once all western Bengalis were called Gaudiyas; today the name belongs to the Vaishnavas, the followers of Mahaprabhu.
  4. In its chapter on Sanatana this biography calls him “Subuddhi Raya, who formerly served Hussain Shah.” In the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 25.180) and in the same biography's chapter on Subuddhi himself it is the other way round: Hussain served under Subuddhi. We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  5. One of the biographies writes that this happened “soon” and calls him Alauddin Hussain Shah, who ruled in 1493–1519. These are historians' data; the “Charitamrita” names neither the interval nor the years.
  6. In the “Charitamrita” the Shah says, “If his caste is taken, he will not survive” (Madhya 25.185); the biographies give his words as “deprived of caste, he will take his own life” and “that is as good as killing him,” and do not quote the Shah's words about his patron, “a father to me” (25.184). One of them says simply that the Shah “made him drink water.”
  7. One of the biographies adds, citing the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” that in such cases the usual prescription was to enter a slowly smouldering fire of husks (tushanala).
  8. According to one of the biographies, mustard oil.
  9. In its chapter on Subuddhi one of the biographies writes the reverse: Rupa took Subuddhi with him and showed him the sites where the pastimes of Vraja took place; in its chapter on Rupa the same biography says that Rupa went round the twelve forests taking Subuddhi with him. We follow the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 25.200): it was Subuddhi who showed the forests.
  10. One of the biographies writes that Sanatana went from Prayaga to Mathura by the royal road while the Lord was returning from Vrindavana by the road along the Ganga — and that this is why they did not meet. According to the “Charitamrita,” Sanatana set out only after meeting the Lord in Kashi, when the Lord had left for Puri (Madhya 25.175–178, 25.203), and it was not the Lord but Rupa and Anupama whom he missed (25.205).
  11. According to one of the biographies, Sanatana met Subuddhi “on reaching Vrindavana”; according to the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 25.204), as also the other biographies, it was in Mathura.
  12. One of the biographies writes that Subuddhi, following the Lord's instruction, “atoned for his past sins by chanting Hare Krishna” and, barely keeping himself by selling firewood, helped the Vaishnavas who came from Bengal. This is inexact: according to the “Charitamrita” the Lord enjoined on him the sankirtana of Krishna's name, and its goal is Krishna's feet, not the cancelling of sins, which depart at the mere semblance of the Name (Madhya 25.191–193). Subuddhi lived by chanting the Name at the Lord's bidding.
  13. The same biography adds that Sanatana went round the twelve forests of Vraja together with Subuddhi and a Sanodiya brahmana and learned from them that Rupa and Anupama had made that circuit shortly before and left by the road along the Ganga. This is not in the “Charitamrita”: Sanatana learned of his brothers from Subuddhi in Mathura and wandered the forests of Vraja alone (Madhya 25.204–208); the Sanodiya brahmana was the guide of the Lord Himself in Vraja (Madhya 17–18).
  14. None of these sources says outright that Subuddhi Mishra is Subuddhi Raya, and the biographies do not give him the name “Mishra.” In favour of the identification are time and place: Subuddhi Mishra is found in Vrindavana before Rupa's arrival, just as Subuddhi Raya is in the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 25.179). But there was also a Subuddhi Mishra among the devotees of Puri (see note 1).
